Your Credit File Before a Mortgage Application

What a mortgage underwriter reads that a loan underwriter doesn't, why timing your applications matters, and the searches that quietly count against you.

A mortgage underwriter and a personal loan underwriter look at the same credit file and read different things from it. Understanding that difference is worth more than any generic "improve your credit score" advice, because it tells you what to actually do, and when to do it.

There's no such thing as your credit score

The number a credit reference agency shows you is that agency's own marketing product. No lender uses it. Lenders build their own scorecards from the underlying data, weight the factors themselves, and reach their own conclusions. Two lenders can look at one file on the same afternoon and disagree completely.

So the useful work isn't raising a number. It's making sure the underlying data says what you want it to say.

What a mortgage lender weighs more heavily than a loan lender

  • Stability over time. A loan decision is largely about the present. A mortgage decision is a bet on twenty-five years, so long-standing accounts, a settled address history and continuous employment all count for more.
  • Every committed monthly payment. Not just whether you pay, but what you've promised to pay. This is the affordability calculation, and it's where existing loans do their damage — the arithmetic is here.
  • Recent applications. A cluster of hard searches in the months before a mortgage application reads as someone under financial pressure, whether or not that's true, and whether or not you were accepted.
  • Where the deposit came from. Anti-money-laundering rules mean large recent credits into your account will be questioned. A gift needs a letter; a loan used as a deposit is usually fatal to the application, and lenders are good at spotting one.
  • The current account itself. Bank statements typically get read by a human. Gambling transactions, regular unarranged overdraft use and returned direct debits all register, and none of them show up on a credit file at all.

Hard searches, soft searches, and the difference

A soft search — an eligibility check, or looking at your own file — is visible only to you, and affects nothing. A hard search is recorded when you formally apply for credit, is visible to other lenders, and stays visible for around a year.

One hard search on its own is unremarkable. Five in three months is a pattern, and it suggests either that you keep needing credit or that you keep being declined. Both readings hurt you.

A few practical rules follow from that:

  • Use eligibility checkers, which are soft, before applying for anything.
  • Skip "shopping around" by making real applications; use the checkers instead.
  • Leave a clear run — ideally six months, minimum three — between your last credit application and your mortgage application.
  • If you're applying for several things at once, track them: the application tracker exists for precisely this, and it stores everything in your own browser.

The six-month plan

If you have half a year before you apply, here's the order to work through it.

  1. Month one: get all three files. Experian, Equifax and TransUnion hold different data, and lenders don't all use the same one. You have a statutory right of access. Check every account, every address, and every date.
  2. Month one: dispute anything wrong. Errors are common — a settled debt still showing a balance, an account that was never yours, an address you never lived at. Agencies have to investigate, and this is the single highest- return action available, and it costs nothing.
  3. Month two: get on the electoral roll. Lenders use it to confirm you are who and where you say you are. Not being registered causes a surprising amount of friction.
  4. Months two to five: bring balances down, especially on cards. Utilisation — your balance against your limit — matters, and it updates monthly. Getting well below your limits shows up within a couple of cycles.
  5. Months two to five: clear the small, fast-repaying debts. Not the biggest ones. The ones with the highest monthly payment relative to the balance, because those are the ones costing you the most borrowing power per pound it takes to clear them.
  6. Throughout: apply for nothing. No cards, no car, no buy now pay later, no phone contract you could pay for outright instead.
  7. Throughout: never miss a payment. One missed payment can undo several months of everything above. Set up direct debits for at least the minimum, on everything.
  8. Month six: clean statements. Assume a human will read three months of your current account, because one will.

Don't close old accounts to tidy up. A credit card you've held for eleven years and don't use is an asset on your file — long history, available credit, no balance. Closing it shortens your history and raises your utilisation ratio at a stroke. Empty it, and keep it open.

If something on your file is genuinely bad

Defaults, county court judgments and arrangements to pay stay on your file for six years from the date they're recorded. You can't remove accurate adverse data, and any firm promising to do that is selling you something worthless.

What you can do is understand how it ages. Most lenders care far more about a default from eight months ago than one from four years ago, and several will lend normally once adverse data is three or more years old and everything since has been clean. There are also lenders who specialise in exactly this situation, at a price.

So the answer to "I have a default, can I get a mortgage" is usually yes, and the useful questions become when and at what rate — which is territory where a broker earns their fee, because knowing which lenders take which view of which adverse data is the whole job.
